item.title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 5: Hibernate Tuning
item.description:
In Part 1 we watched Spring Data's saveAll() take 7x longer than batched persist() because every entity triggers a SELECT before its INSERT. In Part 2 we switched to raw JDBC and cut the time further. But Hibernate still sits well behind — so how close can it actually get to the bare metal?

Three settings close 80% of the gap: implement Persistable to kill the pre-INSERT SELECTs (8x faster saveAll), use StatelessSession to drop the first-level cache (35% faster persist), and layer useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true on top (another 2–2.5x). Combined with proper batch sizing, this is as fast as Hibernate gets.

item.title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 6: Parallel Threads
item.description:
Every strategy we've tested so far — Hibernate, JDBC, Bulk API — pushes data through a single connection. SQL Server handles concurrent writes just fine; the bottleneck is the serial nature of one TCP stream. Split 100k rows across 4 threads with 4 connections and the Bulk API drops from 492 ms to 330 ms, the fastest Java-client result in the whole series.

But parallelism isn't a free lunch — threads past 4 give diminishing returns, concurrent readers slow the writers 2.5x, and the TABLOCK hint changes the trade-off. Here's where the inflection points actually are.

item.title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 7: Index Impact
item.description:
Every production table has indexes. Every INSERT has to maintain them. Add 5 non-clustered indexes to a table and the Bulk API — the fastest single-thread strategy — slows down 7x. The other strategies converge: with enough indexes, the choice of insert strategy stops mattering because index maintenance dominates.

But that's only the start. The surrounding table design decisions matter as much: row width, compression, columnstore, fill factor, GUID vs INT keys, change tracking, temporal history, JSON/XML indexes, statistics auto-update, encryption, and so on all impose their own INSERT tax — and some of them are counter-intuitive (compression makes inserts slower; stats OFF makes them slower; sparse columns are worse than nothing when filled).

item.title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 8: TVP, JDBC, Final Ranking
item.description:
Executive Summary

This series benchmarks 110+ insert strategies and tuning knobs on SQL Server 2025 Express (Windows, Java 17, Spring Boot 3.3) over 4,222 individual benchmark runs. Here's the TL;DR:

The 10 highest-impact decisions (in order)

# Choice Impact
1 Batch your inserts (any strategy ≫ auto-commit per row) 15x
2 Use the Bulk Copy API (SQLServerBulkCopy / insertBulk...) 5-6x vs plain JDBC
3 Parallelize across 4 connections 2-3x on top of #2
4 Enable useBulkCopyForBatchInsert=true in the JDBC URL 2-2.5x
5 Use multi-value INSERT (200 values/statement) 4-5x for JDBC
6 Drop/disable non-essential indexes before bulk loads up to 7x
7 Pick the right batch size (500-1000) — not 10, not 10,000 4-5x vs tiny batches
8 Add WITH (TABLOCK) hint for dedicated bulk-load windows 1.3x
9 Use Persistable + isNew=true if you must use Spring Data saveAll 8x
10 Keep AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS = ON (don't try to be clever) 1.5x

Top 7 counter-intuitive findings

  1. OPTION (RECOMPILE) makes batched inserts 52x slower (2.4 minutes vs 3 seconds).
  2. Delayed Durability = FORCED makes bulk inserts 49% SLOWER, not faster. It helps many-small-commits workloads, not single-large-transaction bulk loads.
  3. Natively compiled stored procs are 21x slower when called from Java per-row via addBatch. Their design assumes the C#/.NET memory-table API.
  4. In-Memory OLTP tables don't help batched Java inserts. They shine for concurrency, not batch throughput.
  5. ROW/PAGE compression make inserts slower (+7%/+33%). Compression is a read optimization.
  6. BCP utility is slower than Java Bulk API when data is in-memory. The file I/O overhead dominates.
  7. AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS = OFF makes inserts 50% SLOWER, not faster. The optimizer needs stats even for simple INSERTs.

item.title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 4: Bulk Copy Flag
item.description:
In previous discussions, we established that bulk insert and multi-value batched inserts represent the fastest methods for inserting data into an MS SQL Server database. However, before concluding this series, let's explore another option.

MS SQL Server has introduced the parameter useBulkCopyForBatchInsert, which automatically activates the bulk API for batched inserts. This functionality operates at the database driver level, enabling it to work seamlessly with both regular parameterized inserts and Hibernate inserts.

item.title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts — Part 3: Multi-Value INSERT
item.description: In a previous post, we concluded that the Bulk API insert is the fastest way to insert data into an MS SQL Server database if the batch size is reasonably large. For Jdbc Template inserts, we created a regular insert statement in the form of insert into table (c1, c2, c3) values (v1, v2, v3), where c1, c2, and c3 are column names, and v1, v2, and v3 are values.

item.title: Fastest MS SQL Inserts in Java — Part 1: Hibernate Batching
item.description:
Introduction

Currently, my team is focused on optimizing the performance of our web services. Our data manipulation tasks primarily rely on Hibernate for interacting with our MS SQL Server database. Hibernate provides a convenient and straightforward API for handling data, particularly for persisting individual or interconnected objects (object graph). However, when it comes to bulk operations, Hibernate's default behavior may not be as efficient. To address this, you can enhance performance by enabling Hibernate batching in the application.properties file.
